summary: ORBITAL FORGE is an interactive, bilingual (EN/ES) space mission design simulator that translates NASA JPL's Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1–5) and real SWaP-C trade-offs into an accessible engineering sandbox. Players design spacecraft architectures across 4 mission segments, balance mass, power, and thermal budgets, validate their trajectories against NASA GMAT R2026a astrodynamics benchmarks (3,673 m/s Hohmann transfer), and survive in-flight operational crises. By bridging academic concepts with GSFC-STD-1000 GOLD Rules and DSN telecom standards, ORBITAL FORGE democratizes flight system engineering for the next generation of mission architects.

ORBITAL FORGE — Technical Synthesis & Submission Narrative (from NotebookLM)

Detailed Engineering & Mission Architecture Narrative

ORBITAL FORGE translates institutional spaceflight standards directly into deterministic simulation mechanics by converting the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook resource definitions into a live accounting engine where Current Best Estimates (CBE) and Mass Growth Allowances (MGA) dictate whether a design passes formal gateway milestones. Rather than treating technical margins as abstract text, our platform programmatically enforces GSFC-STD-1000 ("GOLD Rules") by auditing subsystem architectures against mandatory threshold gates—such as the requirement to identify and eliminate Single Point Failures (Rule 1.05), maintaining a ≥25%\ge 25\%≥25% to 35%35\%35% technical margin pool for mass and electrical power at the Mission Concept Review (MCR / CML 5), and verifying RF link viability. Ground communication budgets are governed by actual DSN Telecommunications Link Design Handbook (DSN 810-005) and Near Space Network (NSN) metrics, dynamically calculating space loss, frequency-dependent atmospheric attenuation, and receiver figure-of-merit (G/TG/TG/T) to verify that downlinks achieve the required ≥3 dB\ge 3\text{ dB}≥3 dB margin for deep-space and near-Earth passes.

To ensure astrodynamic rigor beyond closed-form approximations, the engine couples propulsion selection directly to trajectory models validated by the NASA General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT). While basic sizing utilizes Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation, real-world trajectory feasibility depends on the distinct operational regimes of high-thrust chemical systems versus continuous, low-thrust electric propulsion modules. By integrating mission profiles derived from GMAT's enterprise flight mechanics—incorporating higher-order planetary spherical harmonics, solar radiation pressure perturbations, and multi-body gravitational mechanics—ORBITAL FORGE verifies that a student's chosen propulsion subsystem and propellant mass budget provide the exact Delta-V (ΔV\Delta VΔV) profile and thrust margins required to achieve orbit insertion and halo station-keeping across LEO, Lunar, Lagrange L2L_2L2​, and Deep Space regimes.

This interactive architecture directly resolves the recognized educational dilemma in space science, where academic learning is historically compartmentalized into isolated topics such as orbital mechanics or CAD modeling without demonstrating how decisions interact across a complete mission system. By organizing progression through JPL's Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1 to CML 5) and simulating the concurrent engineering workflows of JPL Team X and NASA Ames MDC, students experience the exact trade-offs faced by actual flight programs. Whether balancing the extreme pointing requirements of Canada's JWST Fine Guidance Sensor, the formation-flying plasma bursts of TRACERS, or the strict rideshare mass envelopes of Lunar Trailblazer, participants stop performing disconnected homework calculations and instead master the multi-segment engineering synthesis demanded of future NASA and CSA mission architects.
